research_decisions.question: The assigned candidate (schedule-sparsity-aware monitoring decision rule) rests on a premise that D1 refuted. Is the replacement candidate — a reliability-based inspection stopping rule using rho = s2_between/(s2_between+s2_est) as the moderator of marginal inspection value — a Q1-level method, or another measurement? Should the line close with an auditable negative?
research_decisions.decision: NO-GO / CLOSE_CURRENT_RELIABILITY_METHOD_CANDIDATE. Do not run the rho test. Retain the inspection-budget results as a bounded retrospective finding, explicitly NOT as a claim that additional inspections contain no information. Reopen only with a separately specified, loss-specific sequential acquisition model that beats a Bayesian value-of-information comparator in a chronological held-out-condition policy replay.
research_decisions.rationale: Codex returned NO-GO and, independently, identified three defects in my own proposed test that I verified on reading: (1) D6's outcome arm is base+[soh_first,soh_last], which endpoint-preserving thinning leaves exactly invariant, so the correlation would be against a constant — the same error class as D3 v1; (2) my directional prediction was analytically inverted — for B~N(mu,tau^2) observed with noise v, reducing v to a*v gives relative risk reduction rho(1-a)/[rho+a(1-rho)], which increases with rho, so HIGH-reliability conditions benefit more, not less; (3) var(slope)=sigma^2/S_xx, and with fixed endpoints adding the midpoint changes neither S_xx nor the slope, so the v2=2*v4 conversion is unjustified. Codex also flagged unresolved normalization-reference timing in the ISU loader (ref = nanmax(v[:L]) uses the full trajectory) and directly relevant prior art: Kim, Choi & Kim 2022 derive inspection schedules from reducible prediction uncertainty and apply them to NASA battery data; Morato et al. 2022 optimise inspection/maintenance planning from updated uncertainty. Uncertainty-reduction plus an economic purchasing threshold is therefore occupied.

research_decisions.question: The pre-registered 18-cell temporal policy replay is complete: 14 NEGATIVE, 4 INCONCLUSIVE, 0 SUPPORT; the primary setting excludes the registered practical benefit and the candidate loses to the fixed schedule. Is there a genuinely executable new inspection policy, does the candidate beat the strongest fixed schedule and ordinary VoI, is any advantage mechanistic, is it statistically and practically significant, can it form an IEEE TIM-level contribution, and does the data support the paper's main claims?
research_decisions.decision: CLOSED. The adaptive inspection-timing direction is closed as a methodological main line. Adjudication on the six questions: (1) executable YES, scientifically new NOT ESTABLISHED; (2) candidate beats neither the strongest fixed schedule nor VoI; (3) no mechanism advantage demonstrated; (4) no positive support, informative evidence against the registered practical benefit; (5) NOT an IEEE TIM-level contribution; (6) data sufficient for the restricted negative, not for a positive method claim. Pivot ranking: B (clock discrimination) first but only as an identifiability gate; A (design sets the error) downgraded to a diagnostic.
research_decisions.rationale: The frozen primary comparison excludes the registered practical benefit for both the candidate and VoI, and across 18 settings there is no supporting result while the candidate generally performs worse than VoI. Crucially the six identifiability gates all passed, so this is a negative result from an identified design rather than an invalid experiment: the action space is real (oracle headroom 21.7-38.9% of decision loss, 29.8% of total J) but an online policy captures only 3.0% of it, which is the hindsight-luck versus predictable-signal separation the cross-fitted statistic was designed to measure. Codex also corrected three of my reporting defects, which I fixed numerically: the oracle gap must be reported against total J (29.8%) not only against decision loss (31.3%); the Candidate-minus-VoI comparison must use the paired interval (mean +3.91 d, CI [-1.17,+11.43]) not the difference of marginal medians, so inferiority is not established; and the four inconclusive settings are inconclusive because interval width relative to margin is large, not because the margin grew. Both pivot candidates then failed their gates: B is structurally unidentifiable because the ISU records contain no cycle-count and no measured-throughput field, and A was downgraded because sigma*sqrt(1+h) is a prediction-error standard deviation rather than a predictor of realised absolute error, its held-out leverage definition is wrong, and applying classical leverage theory is not itself a new mechanism.
